item.text: {"question_id":"6B.7","answer":"Only partially and primarily at the formal-design level. In 2023, Bolsa Família rules used stated income eligibility, protected qualifying families for up to 24 months after income increases, defined benefits as rights of eligible families, required public beneficiary information and local social control, prohibited punitive or humiliating responses to conditionality failures, and created federal inspection, management-quality, and accountability mechanisms (BATCH-0019-E002; BATCH-0019-E003; BATCH-0019-E004; BATCH-0019-E005). Minha Casa, Minha Vida specified income-based eligibility, local selection subject to federal criteria, and priorities for vulnerable groups, including people with disabilities, older people, children, disaster-displaced households, people experiencing homelessness, domestic-violence survivors, and traditional and quilombola communities (BATCH-0019-E018). However, the supplied record does not establish that these safeguards operated effectively in practice, nor does it provide meaningful evidence on appeals, permits, jobs, food distribution, or political punishment. Administrative neutrality was weakened by substantial CadÚnico inconsistencies, an audit estimate that 22.5% of beneficiary families did not meet requirements, possible inclusion of 2.2 million excess families, weak supervision and municipal execution, and a benefit design that continued to favor single-person families; these findings concern administration and equity, not proven partisan targeting, and some defects were inherited from Auxílio Brasil (BATCH-0003-E008; BATCH-0003-E009; BATCH-0003-E011; BATCH-0003-E013). The best-supported conclusion is therefore that formal rules created some barriers against arbitrary or humiliating allocation, but the evidence is insufficient to conclude that welfare and housing were effectively insulated from favoritism or punishment across the broader domains named in the
